strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem (data-efficient instruction tuning) and proposes a forward-only alternative to expensive gradient/Hessian-based influence methods, which is a meaningful efficiency contribution if the quality claims hold.

Experimental scope is fairly broad: multiple target tasks (CommonsenseQA, SocialIQA, HellaSwag, GSM8K), multiple base models (1B-8B, different families), cross-model/scale transfer experiments, length-bias analysis, task-adaptive selection analysis, and a hyperparameter ablation table.

The asymptotic cost analysis (Table 4) clearly situates TRIM relative to LESS/TAGCOS/S2L/RDS in terms of backward passes and checkpoints required, providing a reasonably principled efficiency argument.

The out-of-domain GSM8K experiment (Section 4.2) is a nice stress test showing the method can retrieve structurally relevant (COT) data from a generic pool without topical overlap, which is a more convincing test of the token-matching hypothesis than in-domain results alone.
Reasonably detailed appendices (algorithm pseudocode, hyperparameters, dataset/eval protocol) support reproducibility to a degree, and licenses/tooling are documented.
weaknesses: A central design choice — fingerprints are defined per literal vocabulary token/class rather than by semantic/contextual clusters — raises concerns about what the method is actually capturing. With only 5-10 validation examples, the fingerprint dictionary will cover a very small fraction of the vocabulary, meaning most candidate tokens will fall back to the nearest-embedding backoff mechanism (Eq. 11-12) with a fixed penalty; the paper does not report or ablate the fingerprint coverage rate, so it is unclear how much of the reported performance is driven by genuine token-level 'fingerprint' matching versus this backoff behaving like a coarse static-embedding similarity measure.

No code release is mentioned, and while hyperparameters are documented, the complexity of the token-scoring/backoff/pooling pipeline (several hyperparameters: wQ, wK, wµ, wm, λ, η, layer count, scope) makes independent reproduction non-trivial without released code.

Full-data fine-tuning baselines are sometimes quite weak (e.g., 30.25% on GSM8K, 47.27% average on the multiple-choice suite), which inflates the apparent significance of 'exceeding full-data' claims; it is unclear whether these full-data baselines represent well-tuned upper bounds or under-trained references (e.g., due to LoRA-only tuning, fixed epoch count, or unoptimized hyperparameters).

Results are based on only 3 seeds with modest reported standard deviations, and several comparisons between TRIM and the next-best baseline (e.g., 45.37 vs 44.21 average accuracy) are numerically close; no statistical significance testing is provided to substantiate that these differences are robust rather than noise.

Evaluation scale is limited to relatively small models (1B-8B) and a specific fixed instruction pool (270k examples from four sources); it is unclear whether the method's benefits persist at larger model/corpus scales typical of modern instruction-tuning pipelines, or whether the attention-based saliency signal remains informative when models grow substantially larger or when warmup is skipped/shortened.

The claim of being 'to our knowledge the first token-level, representation-centric data-selection method' is somewhat undercut by the paper's own related-work discussion of LADM and T-SHIRT, which are also token-centric; the distinction from these works, while argued, could be tested empirically with a direct comparison rather than only qualitative discussion.

The warmup phase (5% random subset fine-tuning) required before scoring is a nontrivial and possibly confounding cost/step shared across most baselines and TRIM, but its sensitivity (e.g., how warmup subset choice or size affects TRIM's fingerprints and final coreset quality) is not analyzed, despite fingerprints depending directly on Mwarmup's representations.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important problem (expensive gradient/Hessian-based data selection) and proposes a conceptually interesting forward-only, token-level alternative that avoids backward passes entirely.

The experimental protocol is reasonably broad: budgeted accuracy curves, an out-of-domain math-reasoning stress test, cross-model/cross-scale transfer, length-bias analysis, and task-adaptive subset-distribution analysis all probe different facets of the method.
The write-up is clear and well organized, with explicit algorithmic pseudocode (Appendix B) and an asymptotic cost comparison (Table 4) that at least qualitatively justifies the efficiency claim.
Ablations over several hyperparameters (OOV penalty, pooling, checkpoint choice, number of layers) are provided, showing the design choices are not arbitrary.
The GSM8K out-of-domain experiment is a compelling stress test of the core hypothesis that token-level structural matching can transfer reasoning style across topically dissimilar corpora.
weaknesses: The headline comparisons are run only on very small models (LLaMA-3.2-1B for most tasks, LLaMA-2-7B for GSM8K) with LoRA fine-tuning; it is unclear whether the gains (often ~1 point in Table 1) persist with full fine-tuning or larger/more modern backbones, limiting the significance of the claimed 'state-of-the-art' result.

Several strong, directly relevant baselines discussed at length in the related work (DataInf, In2Core, STAFF, GREATS, TSDS, PDS, DUAL, BIDS) are omitted from the actual experiments; the comparison set is restricted to older/weaker methods (LESS, TAGCOS, S2L, RDS, CLD, BM25, DSIR), which weakens the 'outperforms SOTA' claim.

The efficiency claim ('orders of magnitude faster') is only supported by an asymptotic big-O analysis (Table 4/Section 5); no actual wall-clock or GPU-hour measurements are reported anywhere in the paper, despite this being central to the paper's value proposition.

The token-fingerprint design assigns one fingerprint per vocabulary token class, aggregated (saliency-weighted) across all occurrences in the small target set. This conflates genuinely different contextual usages of the same token (e.g., polysemous words) into a single average representation, which seems in tension with the paper's claim of leveraging 'contextualized' representations and is not empirically validated against context-sensitive alternatives.

Results rely on extremely small target validation sets (5-10 examples), and no analysis is given of selection variance when different sets of 5-10 target examples are drawn (e.g., multiple random target-set seeds); given the small-sample sensitivity typical of few-shot methods, this is a notable reproducibility/robustness gap.

Several improvements over the best baseline are modest relative to reported standard deviations (e.g., Table 1 average 45.37 vs. 44.21 for LESS, HellaSwag 49.08 vs 49.01), raising concerns about statistical significance given only 3 seeds and no significance testing.

Ablations (Table 8) are conducted on a single task (CommonsenseQA) and a single model (LLaMA-3.2-1B), so the generality of the chosen hyperparameters (pooling weights, OOV penalty, layer count) across tasks/architectures is not demonstrated.

The method still requires access to a handful of in-distribution/target-format examples, making it not directly task-agnostic; the comparison against task-agnostic methods (e.g., TAGCOS) is therefore somewhat unfair without controlling for this extra information, and this asymmetry is not sufficiently discussed as a limitation beyond a brief mention.

strengths: The core idea—replacing costly backward-pass gradient/Hessian based influence estimation with a forward-only, token-level attention-derived saliency and fingerprint-matching mechanism—is a genuinely useful and reasonably novel contribution to the coreset-selection literature for instruction tuning.

The empirical evaluation is broad: in-domain multiple-choice reasoning (Table 1), an out-of-domain/low-overlap math transfer test (Table 2), cross-model/cross-scale transferability (Table 3), a length-bias analysis (Fig. 3), and a task-adaptive selection analysis (Fig. 4/5), giving a multi-faceted picture of the method's behavior rather than a single aggregate number.

TRIM consistently beats a reasonably strong and diverse set of baselines (heuristic, training-dynamics, representation-based, and gradient-based methods) across these different evaluation axes, and the out-of-domain GSM8K result (nearly matching full-data fine-tuning from a non-math corpus) is a compelling demonstration of the claimed structural-matching hypothesis.
The asymptotic computational cost analysis (Table 4) is a nice complement to the accuracy results, clarifying precisely why TRIM should be cheaper than checkpoint- or gradient-heavy alternatives.
Reasonable ablations are provided (Table 8) covering penalty factor, pooling strategy, scoring checkpoint, and number of layers, supporting several of the design choices.

The paper is clearly written, the pipeline is explained in good detail with accompanying pseudocode (Appendix B), and related work is thoroughly surveyed and well positioned relative to prior token-centric and influence-based approaches.
weaknesses: Most core experiments use only a 1B-parameter scorer/model (LLaMA-3.2-1B), with only a single larger-scale in-domain comparison (LLaMA-2-7B on GSM8K); broader validation on larger base models or with larger candidate pools (the 270k pool is modest relative to real instruction corpora) would strengthen claims of general applicability.

No wall-clock time or GPU-hour measurements are reported to substantiate the efficiency claims empirically; the paper relies solely on an asymptotic FLOPs analysis (Section 5), which, while informative, does not capture practical overheads (e.g., warmup cost, attention extraction over multiple layers/heads) that could materially affect real-world speedups.

The 'token class' concept is defined purely at the vocabulary/surface-token level (same literal token id maps to one fingerprint regardless of context), which seems in tension with the paper's claim of leveraging 'contextualized' representations; with only 5-10 target samples, class-level fingerprints for common tokens could be derived from very few occurrences, raising concerns about fingerprint stability/noise that are not directly measured.

Sensitivity of the method to the choice/quality of the small target validation set (5-10 samples) is only discussed qualitatively in the Limitations section; no controlled experiment (e.g., varying which 5-10 examples are chosen, or injecting noisy/mismatched examples) is provided to quantify this claimed fragility, despite it being central to the method's practical deployment.

Key hyperparameters (wQ=wK=0.5, wµ=wm=0.5, λ, η) are fixed by convention rather than tuned or justified beyond a limited single-task (CommonsenseQA) ablation; it is unclear how robust these defaults are across the other three tasks or different domains/model families.

Statistical rigor is limited to 3 seeds with standard deviations but no significance testing; some reported gains (e.g., over LESS in Table 1) are within or close to one standard deviation, making it hard to assess whether certain comparisons are statistically meaningful.

The method is not compared against some other recent optimization-based or LLM-judge selection baselines (e.g., GREATS, TSDS, PDS) mentioned in the related work, nor against the token-centric T-SHIRT baseline empirically, despite extensive discussion of these methods in Appendix A; this leaves open how TRIM compares to the full modern competitive landscape.

The claim of being 'the first token-level, representation-centric data-selection method' is somewhat strong given the paper's own discussion of several recent token-centric works (LADM, T-SHIRT), and could be stated more precisely to avoid overclaiming novelty.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel forward-only, token-level coreset selection mechanism (attention-derived saliency + fingerprint matching) that avoids the expensive backward passes required by gradient/influence-based selectors such as LESS and TAGCOS, with a clear asymptotic and measured wall-clock efficiency advantage (Table 5, ~8x faster than LESS, ~20x faster than S2L).

Extensive empirical coverage: main reasoning benchmarks (MMLU/BBH/TyDiQA), a deliberately challenging low-overlap downstream task (GSM8K selection from a non-math pool), cross-model/cross-scale transferability (7B scorer to 13B and Mistral, plus an additional 1B-to-8B/Mistral suite in the appendix), length-bias analysis, and an in-domain selection setting without external targets.

Extensive and honest ablations in the appendix covering number of attention layers used, pooling strategy, IDF reweighting, NFF fallback penalty, checkpoint choice, target-set size sensitivity, and robustness to noisy targets, which supports reproducibility and gives insight into which design choices matter.

The length-bias analysis (Figure 3) provides a plausible and interpretable explanation for why token-centric scoring differs qualitatively from sample-level gradient methods, going beyond simple accuracy tables.
Reasonably complete reproducibility support: full pseudocode (Algorithms 1-3), detailed hyperparameters, dataset/evaluation protocol descriptions, and licensing information.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'up to 9% improvement' in the abstract is drawn from a single, favorable low-overlap GSM8K setting (Table 2); on the primary multi-task benchmark (Table 1) TRIM's average (48.56%) is nearly indistinguishable from the strongest baseline LESS (48.27%), and per-task differences are frequently within or close to one standard deviation, so the core claim of consistently outperforming SOTA is not strongly supported by the main results.

In the in-domain selection setting without target examples (Section 4.5, Table 4), TRIM does not outperform S2L or LESS (52.23 vs 52.45 and 65.12 vs 65.45), undermining the generality of the 'consistently outperforms' claim made in the abstract and conclusion.

No statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests across seeds) is reported despite many comparisons being extremely close numerically, making it hard to assess whether reported gains are meaningful rather than noise.

The method introduces several hyperparameters (wQ/wK, wµ/wm, coverage weight η, NFF penalty λ, number of layers L, IDF on/off) that are tuned/ablated primarily on MMLU and then presumably reused elsewhere; there is limited discussion of how sensitive results are to this potential mismatch or whether per-task tuning was needed to achieve reported numbers.

Fingerprints are built at the vocabulary-token-class level; for highly polysemous tokens this could conflate very different contextual usages within a single averaged fingerprint, and the paper does not empirically probe this potential failure mode beyond a brief qualitative token list (Appendix L).

Experiments are restricted to a fairly narrow model range (LLaMA-2-7B as primary backbone, plus smaller transfer studies); no results at larger scale (e.g., 30B+) are provided to demonstrate the efficiency benefits still translate to state-of-the-art-sized models.

The claim that TRIM 'surpasses full-data fine-tuning' is only demonstrated for TyDiQA (and jointly with LESS), not a general property of the method, yet this is emphasized prominently in the abstract/contributions in a way that could be read as more general than it is.

strengths: The core idea of moving from sample-level to token-level, forward-only scoring is a reasonable and potentially useful direction, addressing a real limitation (length/loss-centric bias) of gradient-based coreset methods.

The computational cost analysis (Section 5, Table 5) is thorough, with both asymptotic complexity and measured wall-clock comparisons across methods, clearly demonstrating the efficiency advantage of avoiding backward passes.

Extensive supplementary experiments (appendices G-N) cover hyperparameter ablations, robustness to target-set size/noise, cross-model and cross-scale transfer (7B→13B, 7B→Mistral, 1B→8B), length-bias analysis, and an in-domain selection setting without external targets, showing considerable empirical effort.
The qualitative inspection of fingerprinted tokens and the nearest-fingerprint fallback mechanism (Appendix L) adds some interpretability and helps substantiate the token-level matching intuition.
weaknesses: The headline claim of 'up to 9%' improvement is driven almost entirely by a single narrow setting (GSM8K selected from a non-math pool, Table 2); in the primary, more representative comparison (Table 1, 5% budget across MMLU/BBH/TyDiQA), TRIM's mean accuracy (48.56%) is nearly indistinguishable from the strongest baseline LESS (48.27%), well within reported standard deviations, making the 'consistently outperforms SOTA' framing in the abstract/intro overstated relative to the actual evidence.

Full-data fine-tuning (48.99% average in Table 1) still beats TRIM's 5% coreset (48.56%) on average; the paper's claim of 'exceeding full-data fine-tuning' is true only for TyDiQA specifically, which is a cherry-picked instance rather than a general finding, yet is presented prominently in the abstract and intro as a general result.

Key design choices (equal weights wQ=wK=0.5 for saliency, wμ=wm=0.5 for pooling, use of last-layer hidden states only, IDF reweighting) are justified only by 'for simplicity' rather than principled derivation, and the ablations (Appendix H) show these choices often provide marginal or even negative benefit (e.g., IDF reweighting slightly hurts MMLU accuracy in Table 11), undermining the principled narrative of the method.

The method rests on the assumption that attention weights faithfully indicate token importance/saliency, a claim long debated in the interpretability literature (e.g., 'attention is not explanation'); the paper does not engage with or empirically address this controversy despite building its entire scoring mechanism on raw attention statistics.

Token-class fingerprints are defined at the vocabulary-token level (not contextualized clusters), meaning a single token type receives one fingerprint aggregated across potentially very different contexts in the small target set; this coarse granularity seems in tension with the paper's stated goal of fine-grained, context-sensitive token scoring, and is not analyzed for polysemous or context-dependent tokens.

No statistical significance testing is reported despite many comparisons being within 1 standard deviation of each other; claims of TRIM 'surpassing' or 'matching' baselines are often not clearly distinguishable from noise given the reported variances.

The warmup phase still requires fine-tuning on 5% of data (backward passes), so the 'forward-only' framing understates the true cost of the full pipeline, though this is shared with baselines like LESS and partially acknowledged.

Reliance on a single hardware/implementation setup and base model family (LLaMA/Mistral) for most results limits generalizability claims; broader architectures (e.g., non-causal or MoE models) are not tested, and it is unclear whether baseline hyperparameters were tuned as carefully as TRIM's own extensive hyperparameter sweep, raising concerns about fairness of comparison.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly explained: moving from sample-level, loss-centric scoring to token-level, forward-only attention-derived saliency addresses two concretely identified failure modes (length bias and loss-centric bias) in existing coreset selection methods.

Extremely thorough experimental program: results span multiple base models (LLaMA-2-7B/13B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, LLaMA-3.2-1B, LLaMA-3.1-8B), multiple benchmark families (MMLU, BBH, TyDiQA, GSM8K, CommonsenseQA, SocialIQA, HellaSwag, MathInstruct-based math suite), and multiple coreset budgets, which gives reasonable confidence that the trends are not an artifact of one setting.

The computational cost analysis is both theoretically derived (asymptotic FLOPs accounting for backward passes and checkpoint counts) and empirically validated with wall-clock measurements on a shared hardware/software setup, clearly substantiating the efficiency claim (TRIM ~3-20x faster than gradient-based or trajectory-based baselines).

The challenging downstream-task experiment (Section 4.2, selecting GSM8K-relevant data from a non-math pool) is a genuinely informative stress test that nicely illustrates the value of token-level structural matching over sample-level signals, and the length-bias analysis (Figure 3) directly supports one of the paper's central claims with concrete evidence.

Extensive ablations (number of layers, pooling scheme, IDF reweighting, NFF penalty, checkpoint choice, target-set size, target-set noise) and transferability studies (cross-model/cross-scale, with both small-to-large and in-model oracle comparisons) substantially strengthen the empirical case and aid reproducibility.
The appendix provides algorithmic pseudocode, dataset/license details, and hyperparameters sufficient for a careful reader to reproduce the pipeline.
weaknesses: On the main general-instruction-pool benchmarks (Table 1), TRIM's improvement over the strongest baseline LESS is small (48.56 vs 48.27 mean accuracy) and arguably within noise given the reported standard deviations over only 3 seeds; the headline '9% improvement' claim is driven almost entirely by the single GSM8K out-of-domain selection experiment rather than being representative of the general-purpose setting, which could mislead readers about the typical magnitude of gains.

TRIM is not uniformly the best method across all settings (e.g., it is outperformed or matched closely by LESS on BBH and by the in-model oracle on Mistral for MMLU/BBH in Table 3; LESS/S2L are competitive or slightly better in the in-domain MathInstruct setting of Table 4/20), which tempers the strength of the 'consistently outperforms' framing in the abstract/intro.

'Token classes' are defined at the level of exact vocabulary token identity, which is a fairly coarse, context-free notion of equivalence (ignoring polysemy, sub-word fragmentation, or contextual role); the paper does not discuss how this interacts with BPE fragmentation of rare words, nor provide a deeper analysis of why this granularity is the right level between token-identity and token-context.

Several core hyperparameters (row/column saliency weights wQ=wK=0.5, pooling weights wμ=wm=0.5, NFF penalty λ) are fixed by convention rather than tuned or theoretically justified, and only MMLU-based ablations are provided to support these defaults; it is unclear whether these defaults generalize to very different task types (e.g., generation-heavy vs. classification-heavy).

The method still requires a warmup fine-tuning phase on ~5% of the pool to obtain Mwarmup, similar to LESS/TAGCOS; the efficiency comparison in Section 5, while fair as stated, could more clearly disentangle how much of the total runtime savings come from this shared warmup versus the scoring stage alone, since warmup cost is non-trivial and shared across most baselines.

No explicit discussion of failure modes or a dedicated limitations section in the main text (only in the Impact Statement, focused on ethical/bias concerns rather than methodological limitations such as sensitivity to tokenizer artifacts, generalization beyond few-shot style benchmarks, or scalability of the fingerprint dictionary with vocabulary/task diversity).
